name: Myoglobin
ligand_name: heme (an iron atom held in a porphyrin ring)
fold_note: the globin fold: eight alpha-helices (named A to H) and no beta-sheet
facts: It stores oxygen in muscle; the O2 binds to the iron atom of the heme.
This sperm-whale protein was the first protein structure ever solved (John Kendrew, 1958).
hints: It is small: one chain of about 150 residues.
It comes from the muscle of a diving mammal.
It starts with M and binds oxygen.

name: Hemoglobin (deoxy form)
ligand_name: heme, one per chain (four in total)
fold_note: four globin-fold chains (two alpha, two beta), each made only of alpha-helices
facts: It carries oxygen in red blood cells; the four chains cooperate, so binding one O2 makes the next easier.
This is the deoxy (T-state) form, with no oxygen bound.
hints: It has four chains of two different kinds.
It is found in human red blood cells.
It starts with H and carries oxygen.

name: Ubiquitin
ligand_name: none - a trick question: there is only protein and water
fold_note: the beta-grasp fold: a five-stranded beta-sheet wrapped around one alpha-helix
facts: Cells attach it to other proteins as a tag, most famously to mark them for destruction by the proteasome.
It is only 76 residues long and almost identical in all eukaryotes, from yeast to humans.
hints: It is tiny: 76 residues in one chain.
It is attached to other proteins as a tag.
It starts with U; its name says it is found everywhere.

name: Green fluorescent protein (GFP)
ligand_name: none added - the light-emitting chromophore is built from three of the protein's own residues (65-67) in the centre of the barrel
fold_note: a beta-barrel ('beta-can') of eleven strands with a helix running through its middle
facts: It glows green under blue or UV light, which made it biology's favourite marker for seeing proteins in living cells.
It comes from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2008).
hints: It is one chain shaped like a barrel.
It comes from a jellyfish.
Biologists fuse it to other proteins to see them glow.

name: Lysozyme (hen egg-white)
ligand_name: none - this is the enzyme on its own
fold_note: two lobes, a mostly helical one and one with a small beta-sheet, with the active-site cleft between them (SCOP: alpha+beta; CATH files it under mainly alpha, so both answers are defensible)
facts: It cuts the sugar chains of bacterial cell walls, protecting egg white, tears and saliva.
It was the first enzyme whose structure was solved (David Phillips, 1965).
hints: It is one small chain of 129 residues.
It comes from hen egg white.
It starts with L and breaks bacterial cell walls.

name: Thrombin
ligand_name: PPACK (D-Phe-Pro-Arg chloromethylketone), an inhibitor covalently stuck in the active site
fold_note: two beta-barrels side by side - the trypsin-like serine protease fold
facts: It is the protease at the end of the blood-clotting cascade: it cuts fibrinogen into fibrin.
Its catalytic triad is His57, Asp102 and Ser195 (chymotrypsin numbering).
hints: It has a large and a small chain.
It is an enzyme from human blood.
It starts with T and makes blood clot.

name: Abl tyrosine kinase
ligand_name: imatinib (Gleevec/Glivec, code STI), a cancer drug
fold_note: the protein-kinase fold: a small N-terminal lobe that is mostly beta-sheet and a larger, helical C-terminal lobe, with the drug in the cleft between them
facts: Imatinib locks this kinase in an inactive shape; it transformed the treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
The crystal contains two copies of the kinase domain.
hints: Each copy has two lobes with a small molecule between them.
The small molecule is a famous anti-cancer drug.
It is an enzyme that adds phosphate groups to tyrosines.

name: p53 tumour suppressor (DNA-binding domain) on DNA
ligand_name: a zinc ion in each protein chain (and the DNA double helix it binds)
fold_note: a beta-sandwich (two sheets packed face to face) that holds the loops and helix touching the DNA
facts: p53 switches on genes that stop damaged cells from dividing; it is the most frequently mutated protein in human cancer.
Most cancer mutations hit this DNA-binding domain, e.g. Arg248 and Arg273, which touch the DNA.
hints: Three protein chains sit on a DNA double helix.
It is called the 'guardian of the genome'.
Its name is a letter and a number: its mass in kilodaltons.

name: Streptavidin
fold_note: an eight-stranded antiparallel beta-barrel with the ligand buried at one end
facts: It binds biotin about as tightly as any non-covalent pair known (Kd around 10^-14 M).
That grip makes streptavidin-biotin a standard 'molecular glue' in lab techniques.
hints: It is a small barrel with a small molecule inside.
The small molecule is a vitamin.
It comes from Streptomyces bacteria.

name: Triosephosphate isomerase (TIM)
ligand_name: no real ligand - only sulfate ions from the crystallisation solution
fold_note: the TIM barrel: eight parallel beta-strands in the centre surrounded by eight alpha-helices, the most common enzyme fold
facts: It is a glycolysis enzyme that interconverts DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
It is called a 'perfect enzyme': it works as fast as its substrate can diffuse to it.
hints: It is a dimer; each chain is a barrel.
It works in glycolysis.
A whole fold - a barrel - is named after its three-letter abbreviation.

name: HIV-1 protease
ligand_name: indinavir (Crixivan, code MK1), an anti-HIV drug
fold_note: two identical, mostly beta-sheet chains that form one active site between them, covered by two flexible 'flaps'
facts: The virus needs it to cut its polyproteins into working parts; blocking it stops new viruses from maturing.
Each chain contributes one catalytic aspartate (Asp25), so the enzyme only works as a dimer.
hints: It is two identical small chains with a drug between them.
It comes from a virus.
Drugs against it are part of AIDS therapy.

name: Adenylate kinase
ligand_name: Ap5A, two adenosines joined by five phosphates - it mimics both substrates (ATP and AMP) at once
fold_note: a central parallel beta-sheet with alpha-helices on both sides (a Rossmann-like nucleotide-binding fold) plus two lids that close over the ligand
facts: It keeps the cell's ATP, ADP and AMP in balance: ATP + AMP <-> 2 ADP.
It is a textbook example of induced fit: the lids close when the substrates bind.
hints: Two copies, each wrapped around a long, phosphate-rich molecule.
It comes from E. coli.
It moves a phosphate group between adenine nucleotides.
